title: Criminal Statistics in Baby Murder Court Cases
section: How Bad Maths Ruined Sally Clark’s Life
text:
How Bad Maths Ruined Sally Clark’s Life
In 1999 Sally Clark was trialled, and convicted for the murder of her two infant sons. Both had died from Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS), which is basically the medical term for “I don’t know man, sometimes babies just die”. A key piece of evidence for her conviction was the testament of Professor Roy Meadows, who claimed that the chance of two children of an affluent family dying from SIDS was 1 in 73 million. He found this number by squaring the probability that a child in similar circumstances died from SIDS (1 in 8500). There are two major problems with Meadows Law; the prosecutors fallacy and assumption of independence. Meadows law confuses the probability of “cause given effect” with “effect given cause”. The probability that a single baby dies from SIDS is 1 in 85000, but that wasn’t the case here. Sally Clarks kids had all ready died, and so setting the population to be every baby, alive or dead, would be misleading and incorrect. The population for finding out how likely both kids were to have died from SIDS needed to be compared to other causes of death, by using babies that had died as the population. Meadows law is an excellent example in the importance of a correctly defined population and sample.

title: Criminal Statistics in Baby Murder Court Cases
text:
Defining The Population and Sample
Samples and Populations are two peas in the statistical pod and their relationship is quite simple. Populations define the group we want to understand, and a sample is a random subset of that group which we use it to understand the population. Actually that explanation is a little circular, let me draw it to make it easier to see.
  
Ok that drawing is literally a cycle. Its just as bad as the explanation. I need to fire my illustrator.
  
Anyway, this circular explanation, while slightly annoying, is the essence of the population and sample relationship, and why getting a solid grasp on the difference is difficult. Rather than constantly trying to think about populations and samples in this cyclical way, let’s instead think about the implied population from any given sample. Then we can consider what happens when we try to deviate from it.

title: Criminal Statistics in Baby Murder Court Cases
section: Lindy Chamberlain AKA The “Dingo’s Got My Baby” Lady
text:
Lindy Chamberlain AKA The “Dingo’s Got My Baby” Lady
The “Dingo Ate My Baby” court case is a great example of poor assumptions left right and centre. From a dodgy test for blood to calling in dingo experts from London to the media circus inspiring guilt, the whole thing is an embarrassment to the Australian court system. One of the key arguments against Lindy Chamberlain was that “dingos just don’t attack people”. There was no recorded evidence of a dingo ever severely attacking a person, let alone killing one, and they typically avoided conflict with humans. The story goes, while camping at Uluru, a dingo got into Lindy’s tent, grabbed her baby (Azaria), and ran off into the night. This event had multiple witnesses and logistically made sense. The prosecution argued, that in the 15 minutes Lindy was away from the campsite, she cut her baby’s throat in the boot of her car with nail scissors, stashed the body in a camera bag, hid her baby’s jumpsuit in a dingo lair, used a vial of blood to sprinkle some around the tent, and then went back to the group at the campsite. All in 15 minutes and without getting a drop of blood on her. Seem like an insane story? Well just like Sarah Clark, Lindy Chamberlain was found guilty. During the trial the prosecution had two main points that directed the jury towards a guilty verdict (ignoring the media’s influence) which were both a huge miscarriage of justice and a great case study in a poor jump from a sample to a population.

title: Criminal Statistics in Baby Murder Court Cases
text:
Prosecution Point 1

“Dingos Just Don’t Attack People, and If They Did, It Wouldn’t Look Like This”
The original coronial inquest for the dingo ate my baby case agreed that Azaria was probably taken by dingos. It wasn’t a far fetched idea that the largest predatory mammal in Australia would eat a small weak animal left alone. Dingos were always wild animals, but they had never attacked people before, and this is a large reason that the criminal trial made it’s way to the courts. The Northern Territory police were dissatisfied with the original coronial inquest and had a second inquest done by sending photos of the baby’s jumpsuit to someone in London who said that the incision around the neck of the jumpsuit implied a cut throat. The jumpsuit of Azaria was mostly in tact except for the top button of the jumpsuit. Something many claimed did not line up with a dingo attack. This part of the argument boils down to “Look, we’ve never seen a dingo attack before, BUT IF WE HAD we’re pretty sure it wouldn’t look like this”. Despite only having a sample of dingo behaviour that included no attacking of people, we used it to understand how they would attack people. In other words, the sample size was too small to capture this rare event, but even so it was used to understand a rare event, expanding beyond the limitations of our data.


Where did this Data Come From? Is My Sample Big Enough?
If we have a sample, it needs to be large enough to be an accurate representation of whatever population we are trying to understand. How large is large enough? It depends. For a rare event such as a dingo attack (there are surprisingly few, feel free to google it), you need a VERY large sample. With too small of a dataset the estimated probability of a rare event goes from improbable to impossible. Additionally, regardless of the size of our sample, we cannot use it to understand events that it has no representation for. Sample size is one of the most commonly cited problems in research critiques, but the problem goes much deeper than that. Most statistical tests (each of which have their own assumptions) typically rely on the sample to be REPRESENTATIVE of the population. Which means it needs to be large enough to capture the rarities of the data, and be an accurate, random sample of that population. Usually as statisticians we focus on averages, but outliers have their own value in of themselves. There are two main questions we should ask about our sample, and the prosecution should have asked about dingo attacks.
1. What is this a random sample of?
If you have reason to suspect there might be a difference between all dingo attacks, vs the dingo attacks we know about we cannot fairly say we know the real probability of something like a dingo attack on a person. To think about what we have a sample of, we need to ask what might cause bias, correlation between observations, ect.
  
2. Is this sample big enough?
This is usually important for reliability in our understanding, but that is even more important when trying to figure our if the event we are looking at is impossible or just very rare. Even if our sample is big enough to be representative it also needs to be big enough that we can reliably understand its relationship to other factors.

title: Criminal Statistics in Baby Murder Court Cases
text:
Prosecution Point 2

“This is Baby Blood In Your Car… We Think”
One of the strongest pieces of evidence (still circumstantial which makes the guilty verdict even more embarrassing) was forensic. Basically a test for fetal hemoglobin in the boot of the Chamberlain’s car had it lighting up as a baby blood fountain. What was not discussed at the time of the trial, and what actually later played a key role in exonerating Lindy Chamberlain, was that this test is not conclusive at all. If you want to use the positive results to directly implicate blood, we need to assume the absence of all the other sources of a positive result. Interestingly, one of the substances that could give this test a positive was copper dust. The Chamberlains lived in Mt Isa, a copper mining town. This case of bad science is a perfect example in drawing the wrong conclusions from a sample because our assumptions of whatever method we were using were not fulfilled.


Context is Everything
Every time you do any kind of statistical test, you bring with it a suitcase of assumptions. The type of data, the relationship, ect, ect, most of which goes overlooked. To perform a statistical test without all the assumptions met isn’t a crime, but we need to understand what happens to our results when they are not met. If you are sitting there thinking “oh well that’s just for inference, not for prediction, I’m safe” guess again chump. The issues in assumptions of method and model can mess with your predictions as well.
Lets look to epidemiology to understand this further. The most basic model for prediction infection for diseases is the SIR (susceptible, infected, recovered) model. Basically it just says here is the number of people who could catch the disease, here is the number that have it, and here is the number that have previously had it. The model, while useful, makes several assumption about the interaction of people that are not realistic. For example, by assuming everyone is equally likely to interact with each other and equally likely to catch the disease, it ignores the nuance of social groups. The model has shown before that a high infection rate caused by a single susceptible social group, will lead to massive over prediction for the whole population.   
This leads me to the third important question you should ask yourself when trying to understand what conclusions you can draw from your sample.
3. What are the assumptions of my model, and what happens when they are violated?
This questions essentially follows after the other two, and is slightly different. Now instead of asking a question about the sample, we are asking a question about the underlying variables. This both gives us the ability to construct models that are more accurate to the problem at hand, and understand the context in which our statistic models might fail. Assuming our current sample’s trends will expand beyond the limitations of the data is a fatal flaw of extrapolation.

title: Criminal Statistics in Baby Murder Court Cases
text:
In Conclusion
Both statisticians and legal prosecutors make mistakes all the time, that being said, sometimes they were avoidable. If we simply take a step back, and assessed the limits of our conclusions we could stop many overconfident predictions, and wrongly accused mothers. Before doing any kind of analysis there are a handful of questions we should ask ourselves. What is my data a sample of? Is my sample large enough to capture what I’m investigating? Is my model making ridiculous assumptions about my variables? Is murder REALLY the most likely reason for a fragile baby to die? Ok, maybe less of the last question for statistics, but the other three for sure.

title: A Future Public Disturbance Explains LDA
text:

If you would like to see the correlation that makes me think this, see the figure below:



Despite this clear character flaw which I refuse to talk about further, I have never written an online review of a restaurant. Unsurprisingly from the tone of this post, the experience turned out to be a nightmare. Spending all my money to get the opportunity to wait hours for an onslaught of terrible food, was probably an indicator I had already died and this was some personalized version of hell. Here is a snippet of a review I got halfway through writing, and then forgot about until this very moment.



You could consider my complaints to be wildly privilege and out of touch, but my dog died a year ago, and I would rather relive that than go to this restaurant again. If you are thinking to yourself that I seem to have unhinged emotional responses to slight upsets, you would be correct. So while we are on the topic of out of touch emotional responses, lets talk about Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA).
Back when I learnt about LDA, I had a regularly maintained page in my notes called “LDA is ruining my life”. Every tutorial for about 4 weeks would be me pointing to a section of the page and asking my tutor why all of it worked the way it did, and why I was too stupid to understand it. Ultimately my issue stemmed from one key question: Is LDA a classification or dimension reduction technique; and if its both, how are they related? I never figured it out, and after the exam, I decided it was something for people greater than myself to know. Or I decided it was not my problem any more. The distinction is unimportant. What is important is that a few weeks ago I overheard someone in the department talking about LDA and I had what I can only describe as machine learning based war flashbacks. So, thanks to this conversation, I reopened the page that hurt me to my soul, and made some plots to help me (and by extension you, the person reading this post) finally understand how LDA works. I’m going to break this down into two sections:

How LDA classification works in the 1-dimensional case
How LDA dimension reduction works in the 2-dimensional case and then extends to classification.

For the running example, we are going to look at some restaurant reviews to maintain the theme of “things Harriet has disproportionate emotional reactions to”. If anyone was looking for a sign that I’m running out of ideas, here it is.

title: A Future Public Disturbance Explains LDA
text:
Theory
LDA is pretty straight forward as far as classification models go. Every time we use a classification model, we are implicitly asking “Which of these groups is more probable?”, LDA just does this very literally. If you are unfamiliar with Bayes theorem (that would be alarming but I’m an adult who said “Who’s Cyprus?” to my housemate the other day so I can hardly judge) it looks like this:
\[P(Y=k|X=x) = \frac{P(K=k)P(X=x|K=k)}{P(X=x)}\]
If you don’t have an intuitive sense of Bayes theorem, its actually pretty easy to draw how it works. Lets say we have two groups, and we want to find the probability that an observation belongs to either Class 1 or Class 2 based on our predictors. Since there are two versions of the function (one for Class 1 and one for Class 2), we will have two different possible equations to plot, and so two different densities. To start with, LDA assumes that both classes are normally distributed and have the same variance, so we only need to calculate three things, each of the group means and their shared variance. Once we have these values we can draw the associated normal density, that is \(P(X=x|K=k)\) for each value of K.



This is already looking pretty good, but what if each class is not equally probable? Well, we can make these densities more accurate by scaling them by their relative class probability, i.e. \(P(K=k)\). So lets say that class 2 is much more likely than class 1, then we end up with this:



Then to finish we just scale both of them down so that they follow the probability axioms. That is, we make sure the probability of belonging to Class 1 + the probability of belonging to Class 2 is not not greater than 1.



With that we end up at the equation for Bayes theorem. Unfortunately this theorem does not give us a classification rule, but rather relative probabilities. To make a rule we could calculate this probability for every class, and then classify our observation to whichever class spits out the largest value of this function, but that is a bit tedious. It would be much easier to have a single value where numbers above it are Class 2 and numbers below are Class 1. Lucky for us, the y-axis here gives a probability, which means for values of x where the Class 2 function is higher, Class 2 is more probable, and vice-versa for Class 1. Therefore, the best place to draw our boundary is when the densities overlap, and both classes are equally probable.



This the basics how LDA classifies observations. The only thing to note, is that it doesn’t do this on the scale of your X variable. It will scale X by some constant such that the classification bound drawn above is at 0, and this new scale is called the Linear Discriminant. To make this a little easier to understand, I can give a real example of 1-Dimensional LDA classification.

title: A Future Public Disturbance Explains LDA
text:
Example
While it would be in character for me to sit alone in my room and write hundreds of spiteful restaurant reviews to make a data set, I’m not going to do that. For this analysis I’m going to use a Kaggle data set with about 1000 restaurant reviews, where each observations has two variables; the typed review and a yes/no indicator for whether or not the person liked the food.
Unfortunately if we want to predict if someone liked the food based off their review, the raw version of this data isn’t going to cut it. We need some comparable variables, which means we need a measure of how positive or negative the review is. For this, I’m going to keep it simple, and use a basic sentiment analysis. For those who don’t know, there are several ways to assess the sentiment of a word, i.e. if it has positive or negative feelings associated with it. There are a number of “lexicons” that are just massive data sets that have a word (such as “hate” or “love”) and an associated score for that words sentiment (-5 or +5). I’m going to use two of these for this example; ‘AFINN’ which gives words a score from -5 to 5, and ‘bing’ which rates words as either positive or negative (simplified to 1 or -1 here). To use these as variables in our example data set, I took the average sentiment of the words in the review for that lexicon. Finally we get a dataset with observations that look like this:

Note: These reviews are some of my favourites, they are not a random sample.
Right now, I’m not going to use both of these sentiments. We are still in the one dimensional classification case, so lets stick to the AFINN average. To see how this variable splits the reviews, lets make a density plot of the data similar to the one explained above.









From this plot we can see that these distributions are neither normal, nor have similar variance. You will rarely have data that behaves exactly according to the assumptions. Does this mean we can’t use LDA? Not really, it just means that if (or when) we end up with a boundary that is a bit different to what you would draw yourself, it is probably because of these incorrect assumptions.
If we perform LDA on this data, we can find the coefficient of linear discriminants. Earlier I said that LDA will perform classification on its own scale, and this is how we find it. This value is used the same way it would be in a regression function, where it gives us the coefficients in the formula:
\[x = 2.929\times AverageSentiment_{AFINN}\] Where x is the “linear discriminant” for that review. We can plot this variable (although it is just afinn_sentiment scaled by a constant) with the decision bound at 0 to see what our linear discriminant space looks like:









It looks exactly the same except now the border for a 50% threshold is at 0. You may notice this is not where the densities overlap, and that is because LDA has assumed that distribution for “No” reviews is more spread out than it is. While it isn’t perfect, with this example under our belts we can move onto using LDA for dimension reduction.

title: A Future Public Disturbance Explains LDA
text:
Theory
Now we move onto the dimension reduction aspect of LDA. Remember how in the previous example LDA changed the original variable to make its own scale, LD1? Well, that is the dimension reduction part working, although in that case it wasn’t reducing the dimensionality, just scaling it. LDA dimension reduction is actually very similar to Principal Component Analysis (PCA) dimension reduction, in that it uses eigen-decomposition. To avoid going into some complicated details you can find elsewhere, whenever you read eigen-decomposition just think “we found direction of largest variance, represented it as a line, and projected data onto that line” and you know enough to make it through this post.
In my last post, I explained eigen-decomposition and how it is utilized in PCA, but it is much easier to understand when you to see it working. The animation below depicts a scatter plot of data, with a line that rotates around its centre. This line represents a potential direction for us to project our data onto (i.e. a 1-Dimensional representation). When we did PCA, we wanted to pick the line that has the highest variance, that is, had the fattest distribution when plotted as a density plot, and this animation lets us roughly see when that point is:

 

The point of this is visually show you the value of eigen decomposition. It gives an instant analytical result for what we could try to find with the animation above.
How is this relevant to LDA? Well it also uses an eigen decomposition, but it isn’t as straight forward as the PCA case. Now we have classes that we need to take into account. LDA decomposition works with the goal of minimising the overlap between classes. That is, if we plot the density of the two groups, we want the smallest possible overlap, as shown below.



There are two components of the distributions that come into play when picking this direction: 1) Distance of Class Means. The importance of this bit is pretty obvious. If the two groups are further apart then they have less overlap. Regardless of the features of the data, this will always be an important aspect. 1) Class Variance and Covariance. While having data that is far away is nice, if there is another projection that brings the class means closer, but makes the resulting distribution steeper, it will result in less overlap. Finding a balance between these two components is what allows us to maximise the distance between the two groups, and find the best 1-dimensional projection of the classes. The interaction of these two elements may not be easy to see above, but it will make a lot of sense with some animated examples. In these examples I have added a value called “VarDist” in the corner, I will get to the calculation of this value later, but for right now, know that it represents the interaction of these two components and we are looking to maximise it.
To start, lets take the variance and covariance of the data completely out of the equation and look at a simple case where our variables have no correlation and our classes are just two bivariate normals with different means.

 

The animation shows two distributions that change in central location, but their shape stays the same. Since the scatter plot shape of each group is essentially circular (due to the 0 correlation of the variables), no matter what direction we project the data into the shape (and therefore variance) will be the same. This means we can ignore the variance and focus on maximising the distance between the means. This is achieved by projecting the data on the line that goes through the two group averages. Moving on from this simple example, lets make things more interesting and look at some data where the variables are correlated.

 

Now we can see two forces at play. Just as before, when the line goes through the two means the data is most separated, but this is no longer the only factor we need to consider. The positive correlation means that the direction we project the data onto can now also flatten or steepen the curve. We can no longer use the line that goes through the two means, because if another direction brings the distributions closer, but also significantly decreases the spread, that would be the preferable option. We can see this in example with negative correlation too.

 

Now that we have seen how this works intuitively, we can go through how this is calculated. So, how does LDA perform a decomposition that accounts for these two competing elements? It combines two matrices in the eigen-decomposition, the variance covariance matrix and a matrix of the between group averages.
First we want to minimise the within class variance of the projected data. The first important thing to note is that by the assumptions of LDA, all the classes have identical variance-covariance matrices. Therefore to calculate the matrix, we get the variance-covariance matrix of each isolated class, and then average them. The averaging shouldn’t change the values (if your LDA assumptions are correct), it should just makes the estimate more accurate. This is illustrated in the picture below.



Now that we have this matrix, how do we find the projection that minimises the variance instead of maximises? We just perform an eigen-decomposition on the inverse of the matrix. Now that we have taken care of the spread element of LDA, we can take care of the “separating the means” element. For this we create another matrix for the “between group differences”.
This is just a matrix representation of the distance between the classes which is constructed using the method illustrated below. Much like with the eigen-decomposition of the variance-covariance matrix, how this matrix works is not of major significance.



Since we are trying to maximise this, we do the eigen decomposition on the matrix. Finally, to get the direction we are projecting our data onto, we need to just take the eigen decomposition of the combination of these two matrices, that is the matrix \(\Sigma_V^{-1}\Sigma_B\).
In this case, what is the “VarDist” value that appears in the plots?. Well, when you do an eigen-decomposition it analytically finds the direction that maximises the distance between groups, but instead of solving it analytically, we could also solve it iteratively and just check the product of the group variance and between group difference in the 1 dimensional projection for a series of projections and select the one that maximises this value. That is the value that is shown in the corner of the animated plots and its calculation is shown in the formula below:
\[VarDist=({\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2}})^{-1} \times \sum_{i=1}^2(\bar{x_k}-\bar{x})^2\]
With this information, it should be clear how we get the 1-dimensional representation that best separates the two classes. While a technical understanding is fine, it is easier to see this come together with an example.

title: A Future Public Disturbance Explains LDA
text:
Example
Following on from our example before, let’s add in a second variable, the bing sentiment measure. Now that we have two variables we can plot them together on a scatterplot to see their relation.









This plot gives us a few things to note. First of all, this is clearly not two bivariate normal densities, as LDA will assume. Again, this just means our results will be slightly off. In addition to this there are a lot of 0 values for both the AFINN and bing sentiments. This can occur in two circumstances: 1) none of the words in the review appear in that lexicon because they are all neutral (“I’m uncertain I could call that food”), or 2) if the sentiment scores of the words in the review cancel each other out (e.g. “The food was so good I felt bad eating it”). Since this only impacts the assumptions of LDA we are going to power through.
Just like with the classification, we can perform LDA on this dataset and get a formula that calculates the Linear Discriminant for each review. In this example our coefficients give a function that looks like this:
\[ x = 0.800\times AverageSentiment_{AFINN} + 5.576\times Average Sentiment_{bing}\] Now, instead of the linear discriminant just scaling the variables so the 50/50 probability split is at 0, it is a linear combination of the two variables. How did it get these coefficients? Using the eigen-decomposition described above. Again, we can calculate the linear discriminant of each review, and in doing so, have a 1-dimensional projection of the data. Now that we have two variables, just like with PCA we can interpret their coefficient values. If the values are on the same scale (or you scaled them prior to performing your analysis) then this is a simple step of comparison. Unfortunately I did not do that (I wanted it to be clear which sentiment was which by the scale or I was being lazy, you pick) so instead we can plot it on the previous scatter plot and comment on the steepness of the slope. Below is a plot of the data with the line it is projected onto, as well as the resulting density.
















Since the slope is not steep, we can see that AFINN sentiment contributes more to the dimension reduction than bing does, and is therefore more important when it comes to separating the groups. This is how we interpret the dimension reduction. You can see that I added the decision boundary in too. Once we have a single dimension that our data exist on, the classification is exactly as it was above, drawing the line where the two densities overlap (or not quite when we violate the assumptions).

title: Mario Party: Destroyer of Friendships and Explainer of Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
This is The Blog of a Mario Party Master
In pre-COVID times, my friends and I would gather around for a fun activity called “lets ruin our friendship by taking Mario party way too seriously”. The night always starts with laughter and few drinks, and ends with me standing on a chair, pointing at my closest friends, and screaming “I’m going to make you cry tears you thought were reserved for the death of your mother”. Once the moment has passed it seems a little dramatic, but at the time, we all truly believe that the speed you can get virtual candy out of a jar is an appropriate measure of human worth.




The last thing my friends see before I block them



There are several games that cause spite, but one called “Absent Minded”, pictured below, always sends us into an argument. Basically, you have 3 characters, and a slowly appearing image, and you have to find out which character is absent as the pictures become clearer. The faster you correctly identify, the more points you receive. I have never lost the game. Additionally there are 3 levels of this mini game, and so 3 different ways the images are shown to you: Jumbled Pictures, Blurred Pictures, and One At a Time.
  Example: the “One At a Time” level 
Now, obviously the levels are meant for humans to play, and not for teaching machine learning, but the challenge each level presents gives us an interesting way to view the concepts. The jumbled picture level can show us how our typical machine learning algorithm will view an image. The blurred picture level shows the benefit of using convolutional neural networks, and the one at a time level can go in the trash! Sorry, not every analogy will fit perfectly into a machine learning theory.
  


How Does The Picture Look to a Computer
Before I jump into explaining the concepts, I want to explain how your computer will “see” your image. Statistical models do not have eyes, and so for any picture we want to use, an observation needs to be converted in to a dataset. The process is illustrated below (although the variable size would be each pixel, and not limited by how small I can make my handwriting).
  
First our image is broken up into its individual pixels. For greyscale they are typically given a single number to represent its “darkness”, and colour images are given three different values for red, green, and blue (RGB). This dataset is what will be used to represent your model (although I will use the image rather than the dataset for visualisations).


Part One: The Jumbled Picture Level

Theory: What’s Wrong With What We Already Have
Technically, we could use any other machine learning algorithm to classify an image. We can call these “bag of pixel” methods as they don’t consider the pixels location in the image. They essentially cut the image up into pixels, shake them up in a bag, toss them out, and classify based off these values. Ultimately, the problem with any “bag of pixel” model, is that it fails to capture the shape of the image independent of its location. This means only images that have the right features in the right area are correctly classified.


Analogy: What Makes the Jumbled Level Hard
  
The jumbled picture stage is interesting, because we cannot look at the characters as a whole to identify who is present. Since We cannot identify the pictures using the overall shape of the character, we need to look for the presence of independent key features. This reliance on identifiable features in the correct location is also what identifies our ordinary algorithms.


Putting Them Together
In reality, this jumbling in our pictures would be at a pixel level, not big chunks, but the minigame is more of a point of illustration rather than a technical tool to understand machine learning. Key features being in the right place can be used successfully to identify images, but ultimately we have “zoomed in” too far to see the relationship between pixels. We can conceptualise this further with an example.
If we are trying to identify Mario, cap-looking pixels where Mario’s cap should be make it easy. If we have a picture where Mario doesn’t have his cap, that makes it hard. If we have a single picture where Mario is laying down so his cap is where his feet should be, that makes it even worse.
This is essentially the problem with our regular Machine learning algorithms. Key features in the right place make classification easy. No key features makes classification hard. Key features in uncommon places will be incorrectly assumed to be something else, and cause misclassification. This is where the benefits of using a convolutional neural network come in.



Part 2: The Blurry Image Level


Theory: How does a Convolutional Neural Network Work?
Before we return to explaining machine learning concepts in terms of Mario Party, lets take a step back, and look at how convolutional neural networks work in general. The illustration below is an overview of the structure of a CNN. The information contained in the image undergoes several transformations using layers that can be classified as either “feature extraction”, or “classification”.
  

Feature Extraction Layers
Feature extraction is what really sets the CNN apart from other models. These layers make new variables that are more “computer vision friendly”. The process creates nodes that identify certain aspects of an image, such as Yoshi’s Shell or Peach’s hair, and converts them to variables we can use to make predictions. The most common (and technically interesting) layers used in the process are explained below. The “options” are specifically related to building CNN in the R package, Keras.

Convolutional Layers
  
The convolutional layer is what makes a neural network, a convolutional neural network. This layer creates a small window (called a kernel), that travels along the image and looks for a specific feature. The kernel_size option selects the size of the grid that is run along the image. Larger grids can overlook important details, while smaller grids can provide too much information and create noise. Typically the standard is somewhere in the range of a (3x3) grid. This information is taken from image to feature map using a filter. The filter is basically the type of feature we are looking for, when we run the kernel over the image. The number of times we do this, each with a unique filter, is the “depth” of the layer. In Keras, that is given by the filter option. As for which filters it uses, that is trained by the model.
The only convolutional layer that takes information from the image is the first one. All the following feature maps are computed on the previous feature maps. The new filter is applied to some combination of the previous layers feature maps and thus more convolutional layers mean variables that represent more intricate features.


Max Pooling
   Max Pooling is a step in our convolutional neural network that is essentially a dimension reduction of our feature maps. Literally just think of it as doing no transformation to the image, other than shrinking it down. As with all dimension reductions, the goal here is to get rid of the pixels that contain noise (e.g. white space) and keep the pixels that identify the image (e.g. Mario’s cap). This layer reduces our chance of overfitting, and thus is a key player in the bias and variance trade off in convolutional neural networks.


How does it work?
Just like the original image, feature maps can be seen as a grid of pixels. Max pooling sections each feature map into smaller non-overlapping grids, takes the largest value of those pixels, and moves it on to the next layer. The example illustration above is looking for the darkest pixel on a 2x2 grid. Grid size is important, we want to minimise the bias introduced into the model by keeping the grid small, but also eliminate noise and not make the grid so small the layer does nothing.


Why the Maximum?
Max pooling is a rather counter-intuitive layer, statistically speaking. Through practice, it seems that the maximum is the measure that minimises this information loss, rather than measures of central tendency as we would expect. As to why, the best analogy I’ve seen for the max pooling stage is from the data sceptic podcast. If you are looking for your keys, and everyone in the group says they don’t have them but one person, you aren’t going to take the median or average value. We are not looking for how much the picture looks like Mario’s cap on average, we are looking for any sign of Mario’s cap.



Classification Layers

Dense
A dense layer allows takes the nodes from the previous convolutional layers, and make a fully connected layer. This essentially takes our feature maps as inputs and runs them through a typically neural network, which we won’t go into detail about here. Our final classification layer is also a dense layer, that outputs the probabilities of each classification option. This is the final output of the model.



Dropout Layers
Unlike the previous layers, dropout layers can be placed among the feature extraction or classification layers. In fully connected neural networks its use is quite simple; it samples random nodes to remove from the layer, which prevents overfitting. This interpretation does not follow for dropout layers placed among the feature extraction layers (the reason is matrix multiplication but its not worth going into) however it still helps prevent overfitting. Sometimes the number of pooling layers is limited by the resolution of the image (we can only max pool it to be so small) so if we need an additional measure against overfitting, we can include dropout layers.



Analogy: The Blurry Image Level
  
Circling back to Mario Party, the blurry levels difficulties are different to the jumbled level. Here, we struggle to make out key features, but must use the overall shape and colour to identify the character. As the image becomes clearer, it becomes easier to see, and we are more certain of our answer, however this additional certainty does not come without cost. The longer you wait to select an answer in the minigame, the more likely it is that you lose. This ultimately means that if the differences between characters are too subtle, the amount of time it will take to identify the difference isn’t worth the cost, and we are better off guessing.


Putting It Together
Waiting for certainty in the minigame is similar to overfitting in our convolutional neural networks. The deeper we go, the more likely it is that we overfit, and the more computationally heavy it is. We can add in dropout layers, but eventually there is an upper limit on the certainty we can have in our prediction. Unlike the normal models however, CNNs can capture shape AND the key features, they just need to be deep enough.


Mario Party and Convolutional Neural Networks: A Neat Analogy or Desperate Stretch to Make Statistics Seem Fun?
Obviously the CNNs have more nuance to them than can be explained using a Mario Party minigame, but it doesn’t do a bad job of giving us a conceptual understanding. Normal algorithms are limited by their inability to identify characters independent of their location, an issue we can circumvent using CNNs. CNNs capture the shape and general features of a character. Although really the most important learning experience from this post should be that if you come to my house to play Mario Party you might end up dead in a ditch somewhere.

I know the title is provocative, but hear me out; I say this as someone who has dabbled in a bit of crackpottery myself. Usually I keep my unpopular opinions to myself, but I feel this one might actually offer value. Mostly because I have, once again, read an opinion piece by a senior VIS researcher who is crashing out about the lack of a formal theory in VIS and complaining about the fact that everyone is just kind of doing stuff. For examples of what I am talking about, see this paper, this paper, and literally last year’s keynote for IEEE VIS.
I want to hedge this by saying that my main areas are visual inference, uncertainty visualisation, visualisation information theory, and statistics. I understand this is a small piece of the VIS area (although that in and of itself is part of the problem). So, if you are reading this, and you are thinking “well this doesn’t happen in MY VIS area” then I’m happy for you. There are many VIS fields with consistent epistemic principles, and if that applies to your field, you may go on your merry way.

section: I promise I am not a hater
text:
I promise I am not a hater
My point here is not to suggest that all of VIS research is worthless garbage (I mean, it wouldn’t make sense for me to publish one of my papers at VIS if this was the case). TO really show that I am not a hater, I want to start by mentioning some VIS papers that I really liked. You can skip this if you are already assured of my hater (or non-hater) status.

I think the product plots use of measure theory to connect the geometry and probability of graphics is neat.
I think ggdist is a nice description of mark design for univariate distributions.
I also liked the way Rainbow Colormaps Are Not All Bad and The Risks of Ranking reinvestigated widely held beliefs about plot design
I think utilising grid lines to try and fix the sine illusion in Gridlines Mitigate Sine Illusion in Line Charts is a really interesting way to utilise of what we would have previously considered “chart junk”
I am a big fan of inattentional blindness research (I used to be into behavioural economics so this was a shock to me), so I thought the Jurrasic Mark paper was so clever, especially because shows the danger of a task/inference based approach.
The grammar of graphics says that bar charts should only really be used to show a sum, so I like that Visual Sedimentation finds that perceptual research actually backs that up.
I think Attention and Visual Memory in Visualization and Computer Graphics is is an interesting discussion about how we read plots (that feels better aligned with exploration than some task based research)
I have always thought tests into the seperability of marks, such as Measuring the Separability of Shape, Size, and Color in Scatterplots is really important because many of us (or at least many statisticians) treat them as independent axis.
Similar to the separability work, I really enjoyed this paper, Perceptually Uniform Construction of Illustrative Textures when I saw it as IEEE VIS 2023. The idea that something we map in VIS is actually two different aesthetics that can curve around (i.e. they have that horseshoe shape) is deeply fascinating to me.
I like the recursive structure suggested by gofish and I think it identifies a real fundamental property in the structure of charts that we don’t really talk about.
In general the findings in this Uncertainty in Science is Malleable paper were about what I would expect BUT this paper has the single greatest line I have ever read in a paper and I think about it at least once a week: “After numerous design and implementation iterations for visualization glyphs, our visualization system shows, by default, the uncertainty measures using simply a size encoding. After two years of work, did we simply create a visualization with a set of filters and a representation of uncertainty using size?”. I LOVE the honesty from the authors here, and I am so glad that VIS has a culture that let them keep that sentence in.

NOTE: I will add to this list if I remember or see papers that I really like - and am still updating this post. This is not a complete list, there are other papers I like, but I don’t have all day, people.

section: My personal experience at IEEE VIS 2023
text:
My personal experience at IEEE VIS 2023
Around the start of the second year of my PhD, I was quite involved in the VIS community. Most of my Zotero was filled with IEEE TVCG papers; I picked VIS papers for my research discussions; and I went to VIS 2023 in Melbourne, where I presented an early version of my PhD research as a poster. At this point, my supervisors, who were more statisticians than VIS researchers, were not really keen on my work, but they couldn’t really explain to me what was wrong with it. I was working on a taxonomy that described the information of uncertainty visualisations. From my perspective, my research was quite similar to the research I enjoyed reading in VIS conference proceedings and journals, so I didn’t see what was wrong with it. However, while at VIS in 2023, I started to understand my supervisors’ perspectives and develop some concerns of my own.
Now, I need to give a little context for the issues I ran into at VIS 2023. By training, I am a statistician (with a little bit of economics). That is to say, I approach graphics from a statistical theory perspective. However, I actually think this is a strength for one key reason: data visualisations are literally summaries of data. They are therefore statistics, and their information theory falls under the purview of statistics. The only people who I have found to disagree with this statement are those who want to work on statistical graphics, but are uninterested in learning any statistics, which is going to be an ongoing issue in this post. This drawing is the best explanation I can give for how information must travel in a visual inference task (like it is literally just the fundamental concept of information theory).

This is a very straightforward point: I cannot visualise information that is not in my data, and I cannot see information that is not visualised. At best, the information passing between layers can be equivalent to the stage before, but never more. So the potential amount of information in the visualisation should follow this principle: \(data \subseteq visualisation \subseteq observer\). If we ask someone to perform a specific task, we are indirectly asking them to compute a statistic, \(\omega\), which will have an associated sufficient statistic. A sufficient statistic is a function of a sample that captures all the information about \(\omega\). Therefore, at the very minimum, for a participant to correctly answer a question about a graphic, the graphic must contain (in some form) the sufficient statistic. If you show someone a graphic which does not contain sufficient statistical information it is mathematically impossible to answer the question correctly. No amount of human perception studies will change this fact.

Why is this relevant to VIS 2023? Well, at VIS, I noticed several talks in which the authors compared two different plots on a single task. However, in one plot, the sufficient statistic was intact, while in the other, it had been destroyed. The information required to answer their question was gone before any human looked at the plot. We didn’t need a perceptual experiment to work that out. Additionally, I started to find that computational distance to the sufficient statistic was a near-perfect predictor of every single task-based experiment. Because the authors did not consider the statistical information in the plot, they were constantly attributing the statistical information loss to the human observer, with statements like “our results show that people are unable to extract the mean from a boxplot”.
So, since it’s a conference, and I am a young and enthusiastic PhD student, I decided to try and talk to some of the authors about this observation. I am not an animal so I didn’t raise my “it’s more of a comment than a question” during Q&A, but I did stop the authors after their session to discuss how sufficient statistics could inform their stimuli design. To say that the responses I got from VIS academics were overwhelmingly rude and dismissive is an understatement.
One author stared at me, didn’t answer my question, looked at my name badge, and said with a southern drawl “Mooonaaaaash University” before sniggering and saying “where even is that?” and then turning away to talk to someone else. Another attendee said I was “trying to use statistics to gatekeep visualisation research” and asking people to check if their plot had sufficient statistical information was “an unfair burden to put on VIS researchers”. Another academic said that, as an “expert”, I might read plots that way, “but VIS is interested in understanding how the average person reads plots”, so my theory of information was not useful.



I hate this man


While the rudeness was certainly a problem, the thing that was more concerning to me was the way that everyone was acting as though I had shared an opinion, rather than a mathematical fact. To me, ignoring sufficient statistics in VIS felt like a statistician ignoring the fact that 1+1=2. The entire experience was bizarre, and ultimately soured my attitude to the VIS for the rest of my PhD.

title: If VIS wants rigor, it can’t incentivise crackpot science.
section: Oh no, am I doing crackpot science?
text:
Oh no, am I doing crackpot science?
It was around this time that I saw this video (and also this video) on crackpot science. The video suggests four markers of a crackpot theory:

The work addresses the biggest problems in the field
It is lacking in mathematical rigor, experimental evidence, etc.
When their ideas are rejected, they respond with anger and claim the scientific establishment has blacklisted them
The theories are not recognisable as theories for that field.

Upon seeing this list, I realised why my supervisors (and panel) were not fans of my research. My PhD work had a lot of the markers of a crackpot theory. To translate the crackpot theory to the context of my particular research question, the issue was that:

Trying to describe the information theory of uncertainty visualisation was way too vague and broad. In an effort to be generalisable and far-reaching, the theory said nothing.
By using a taxonomy, I was avoiding mathematical rigor, and designing a theory that was not verifiable or testable in any capacity.
I was not being receptive to my supervisors concerns about the research.
I was not using the established language or theories of statistics, so my research was not recognisable as a statistics theory.




My supervisors search history


Now, I wasn’t running around screaming about being Einstein (that would come later), but there were enough similarities that I started looking more critically at my research. After all, if I really believed my work was different to crackpot shit, I shouldn’t be averse to proving it. It turns out, proving it was much harder than just offering a vague taxonomy, but it also made the work more valuable. Through the mathematical formalisation, my theory went from a vague idea to something that could be tested and falsified (if wrong). What was involved in this process? Specifically I had to:

Drop the taxonomy approach and formalise my ideas in mathematical statistics, which required me to: (a) Argue that visualisations should be considered continuous functions from the data space to the visual space. (b) Define a metric for the visual space, which can be used to define the space of visual graphics as a metric space. (c) Use the metric space to define convergence of statistical graphics. (d) Use convergence to translate continuous mapping theorem to uncertainty visualisations and show their ideal behaviour.
Translate this formal theory into a testable hypothesis that could predict the outcome of an experiment and be falsified by a negative result. A consequence of the mathematical formalisation is that a visual signal should be harder to see as the uncertainty increases.
Actually test this hypothesis with a proper human experiment.

At every stage, I asked myself what a crackpot would do, and then tried to make sure I did the opposite. Ultimately, this approach had the extra benefit of leading to a flexible and generalised uncertainty visualisation system that can make an uncertain version of any plot, called ggdibbler. A result which is clearly of interest to the VIS community, since two papers from this year - i.e. 1 and 2 - make plots that do a similar thing.

title: If VIS wants rigor, it can’t incentivise crackpot science.
section: OK hear me out, I think VIS has a little bit of crackpot stuff too
text:
OK hear me out, I think VIS has a little bit of crackpot stuff too
When I started applying the “crackpot checklist” to my research, I started getting more interest from statisticians and less interest from VIS. Unlike the VIS community who were overwhelmingly dismissive of my comments about mathematical rigor, statisticians were enthusiastic about it. Some might argue that I am being pedantic about the distinction between statistical graphics and VIS, but I would disagree. To start with, nobody in statistics has called me a gatekeeper who went to a shit university (well, not yet). But the other main differences are that (1) statistical graphics builds on a well-established theoretical foundation (statistics), and (2) the primary reviewers for statistical graphics papers are statisticians who can tell if there is something wrong with the statistical logic. If you ignore these differences, you end up with something that starts to look a LITTLE bit like crackpot science. So, lets look at that crackpot list again and discuss each one in relation to VIS (ignoring #3 because we are talking about a whole field).
But before that, I need to give a CLARIFICATION! These examples are not about these authors or their work in particular. You will notice that many authors appear in both the papers I love that were mentioned at the top of the post, and the papers with some questionable decisions (listed below). I mean, I even have a few papers I could split in half into the love and hate category. So, the point of this is not to say that I think these authors, or their work, are “crackpot”. Rather within VIS this is all perfectly good research, which is exactly my point. VIS is not suffering from a handful of crackpot researchers, I think the culture in the field itself promotes the exact qualities (big ideas, vagueness, bespoke methods, etc.) that other fields would consider to be somewhat crackpot.

1. The work addresses the biggest problems in the field
How does VIS view themselves as a field? Well, we can get a gist from this bluesky comment where I was told that “the correct project for VIS is not checking data formalisms against human interpretation, but building up models of how people read charts that combine those data formalisms with perceptual and cognitive operators”.
(Correction: Matt said I misunderstood his comment and he is pro maths formalism and specifics (previously this section had comments on maths formalism). Sorry Matt, my bad. The following section is, from my understanding, not in disagreement with Matt’s comment.)
(Correction 2: I previously said Tamara Munzner agreed with Matt’s point because she liked the post, but she has clarified that she does NOT endorse Matt’s anti task rant )
In conversations, I have noticed a little animosity to the idea of limiting the scope of the VIS. I think a lot of VIS researchers see VIS as a melting pot of a field where they are coming up with a true “theory of visualisation” that can cover everything that visualisation touches. Therefore, the breadth of visualisation is a strength, after all it allows them to take the best ideas from multiple fields, including statistics, computer science, and human psychology.
The problem with this idea, is that it is a bit of a fantasy. When you make a field so broad that it involves everyone, people who do work that is tedious and time-consuming end up outnumbered and ejected from the community. This is the case for statisticians whose field moves slower, so they publish far fewer articles than the average VIS researcher. I rarely come across a formally trained statisticians in VIS, the vast majority of people doing “statistical graphics” in VIS are computer scientists who do not have a large amount of statistical training. This is not a bad thing, I have seen people from all fields, including linguistics, biology, and music do great statistics research. The problem is that these people do statistics in a field of statisticians who can check the correctness of the work.
Having such a broad range of domains means that authors with the expertise required to review a paper is few and far between. This is especially bad when you have the pace difference between the fields as decribed above. I often find myself outnumbered (on both sides of the reviewer-reviee relationship) when I try and correct incorrect statistical reasoning. I have found this to be anecdotally true as I know several statisticians, who have also had their comments shrugged off and treated as a “difference of opinion” rather than a self-evident statistical fact.
This leads me to wonder if the openness at VIS not only prevents the idealised “melting pot” community, but also the persuit of it leads to a reduction in the quality of re.


2. It is lacking in mathematical rigor, experimental evidence, etc.
I have noticed a bit of an aversion to mathematical rigor at VIS (see story above). One thing I find quite odd about this response is that it implies that math is some kind of limitation on the field that would reduce the number or flexibility of the theories. I mean, I would hardly describe the fields within the purview of math, such as the physics of the entire universe, predicting the weather, and describing the economy, to be simple or trivial research. The idea that computer graphics is the one field that is too complicated for math to capture feels a little absurd to me.



Math doesn’t deserve this disrespect


This aversion to formalism leads to what I would call a “statistics slop” issue in VIS. These are papers that have statistical arguments that have the sheen of statistics, but the statistical reasoning is often built on confusing or questionable assumptions, and/or disconnected from standard statistical theory. All the calculations in these papers are often correct, with a logical flow, and they look just like what we would see in a statistics textbook, so on face value, there is no problem. However these papers often fail what I would call the “statistics sniff test”. They are, what some academics might call, “not even wrong”.
Before I give some examples of what I am talking about, I want to make it clear that the authors of these papers are not to blame for this. As a matter of fact, to make this point clear, I want you to read the explanation as to why these papers have incorrect statistical logic and see if you, as a VIS researcher, would have clocked it. These are going to focus on uncertainty visualisation (that is my specific area of expertise and also where statistical reasoning is most relevant) but I have noticed similar issues in papers outside this specific literature. With that being said, here are some examples of the issues I’m talking about:

The MapLineup paper paper, which criticises the lineup protocol, and suggests a different method to measure JND. This paper seems to have been was entirely borne from the authors misunderstanding about the fact that a lineup protocols must has a random null plot with no structure. Actually a lineup can have any null distribution you want. I don’t understand why the authors seem to think that spatial autocorrelation in the null would require a different method. They do not provide any justification for this in the paper.
This Evaluating the Use of Uncertainty Visualisations for Imputations of Data Missing At Random in Scatterplots paper, which is visualising imputed missing random values, using things like confidence intervals or density plots. The confidence intervals are calculated using using the sampling distribution associated with the mean imputation. The proper confidence intervals for the missing values would have been the prediction intervals (which would be far wider than the intervals used in this visualisation). This is because the no-imputation case, is not conditional on the imputation, so by making the confidence intervals dependent on the mean imputation, these plots have two different “ground truth” values. Other than this issue, the statistics in this paper is totally correct (at least on my pass, but I don’t know everything, lol) and since the statistical error is quite subtle, I actually think this one is one of the better ones (and it would pass review at a statistics journal). I thought the experiment was well designed otherwise, and would have been interested in the results of this paper, especially if compared to the “in the gutter” approach from the naniar package. Note: This version incorperates parts of Abhraneel’s rebuttal, which can be found here.
The value suppressing uncertainty palette paper which suggests suggests a 2D palette, which blends colours together as they become more uncertainty. The problem with this, is that really isn’t a sensible way to represent a distribution as a single colour, so there isn’t a statistically sensible way to blend the colours together. You could say it should align with some sort of hypothesis test, but hypothesis tests often don’t agree. For example, if we consider three values, each of them might pass a paired t-test, so they should be the same colour, but fail an f-test, indicating that they shouldn’t be the same colour. How do you set the scale such that this works? You can’t. This issue arises from the fact that this mean/variance approach is a fundamental mischaracterisation of what a random variable is.
The Effects of ensemble and summary displays on interpretations of geospatial uncertainty data. This one is NOT a VIS paper, but it includes some VIS authors, and it is foundational work for uncertainty VIS, so I have included it here. The paper consists of several experiments that assess different approaches for visualising storm uncertainty. Experiment 1 and 2 have conflicting assumptions, which are not acknowledged by the authors, and make for a confusing read. The first experiment sets the ground truth on the assumption that the storm intensity is unrelated to the distance to the center of the distrbution, the third experiment assumes the opposite. I have read this paper three times, and I cannot see another way to interpret this study. (This has driven me insane for years, so if someone can explain what is happening here I would love to find out that I am wrong.) HOWEVER this paper isn’t all bad. The finding that people think an event is more probable if it lands directly on a simulated outcome is very interesting (and the statistical reasoning is correct).
The Fitting Bell Curves to Data Distributions Using Visualization paper asks people to fit a bell curve to a boxplot, histogram, dotplot, and stripline plot. These plots have wildly different statistical information with very little justification linking them. There are also questions about when plots of different resolutions can be compared (but expecting people to understand how resolution affects bias would be beyond completely unreasonable on my part).
The How Visualizing Inferential Uncertainty Can Mislead Readers About Treatment Effects in Scientific Results paper compares people’s sense of uncertainty when shown confidence and prediction intervals. This one is…. confusing to me to say the least. Yes, you will have smaller uncertainty bands when you have a confidence interval. Yes, most people do not know the difference between a confidence interval and a prediction interval. There isn’t a way to compare the the two intervals on an inference question that wouldn’t favour one of the plots. The paper seems to be built on the assumption that you can, or should be able to in some capacity? In this specific case, the participants were making a judgment on a new game outcome, so I think the prediction interval is the correct distribution (but the information to work this out is often hidden away in the methods or appendix of the paper). Given the statistical discrepancy, I cannot wrap my head around the purpose of the human experiment in this paper. This boils down to comparing apples to organges on the basis of which makes better orange juice, and then confirming the results with a human taste test. I also suspect this paper is why I sometimes see VIS papers present a prediction interval (when they should be showing a confidence interval) so that they don’t “underreport the uncertainty”.
The Impact of Vertical Scaling on Normal Probability Density Function Plots paper scales individual density functions and checks it’s impact on the human perception. Like the imputed missing values paper, this paper isn’t particularly ergrigious, but the assumptions of the paper are so alien to me, I just had to include it. Yes, the y-axis on density curves is arbitrary. Yes, it is important to keep the area consistent for if you are comparing distributions (that is the common unit between plots). Yes I understand software allows you to independently scale distributions. The only case where I would scale two distributions differently is if one distribution was so spread out/concentrated it was unreadable, and you are not supposed to compare distributions across independently scaled plots (only within plots). You should never independently scale distributions that are on the same scale. Like the Hofman paper above, I get the impression that the core assumptions required for this paper is the sentiment that “people do statistics wrong”. While I accept that this is probably a fair motivation in the VIS literature, I am often confused as to why this is proven with a human perception study.
The Bar graphs depicting averages are perceptually misinterpreted: The within-the-bar bias again, not a VIS paper, but a lot of VIS papers are related to this, so it is worth mentioning. Bar charts should show a sum. It doesn’t make sense to use a bar to show an average as a bar is an interval. This is even explicitly stated by the grammar of graphics. I am not sure why we need so many human perception studies on the within bar bias and how to correct it, when you shouldn’t have used a bar in the first place.

NOTE: I have added to this list to spead out my criticism and avoid attacking a small handful of authors. I see this as a field level problem, and not due to a few individuals. This is not a complete list and I might update it when I think of papers that should be in this list. If your paper appears in this list and you disagree with my assessment, feel free to post/send me a rebuttal and I will link it to the discussion of your paper.
What is my point with these examples? Well, mathematical rigor extends beyond individual mistakes or calculations, it can also suggest purpose. As a statistician, people assume you mostly deal with bad answers, but you actually spend almost all of your time on bad questions. A bad answer is something like an incorrect statistical model, or maybe a failure to account for assumption violations (like missing values or heteroskedasticity). These issues are often trivial. A bad question is a different issue entirely. Bad questions are vague in what they want, can’t decide how to measure it, and have competing, conflicting, assumptions. When I look at these papers with their bizzare assumptions, confusing distribution choices, and inability to define what they are even trying to test, I do not see a field with bad answers, I see a field with bad questions. The process of defining an idea mathematically allows you to clear up these problems. What do you mean when you say “best”? Do you mean easiest to interpret? Easiest to make? The one with the most information? The mathematical definition of your goal goes back to your core beliefs about what it is the field is trying to do. What does “best” mean to you? If ten papers that all find the “best” design, each have their own definition of best, rooted in completely different views for the field, they will never coalesce into a single cohesive theory. You are doomed to painstakingly troll through the methods and appendix (as I had to do for the papers above), to work out what this papers definition of “best” is. We are not liberated by the avoidance of mathematical specifics, we are shackled by it.
These problems are not limited to the statistical arguments either. Theoretical papers in VIS present ideas for how visualisations are made or used, but are often incredibly vague, and use their own bespoke terminology/symbols and are impossible to translate into the mathematical formalisation required to actually test it. The correctness of these papers seems to be based on how real they “feel”, with the epistemics of the area having more in common with a religion than a science. The most famous version of one of these papers I can think of is a nested model for visualisation (no hate to Tamara though, this is just the main one that always comes to mind). Because of this, the large majority of experimental work do not actually test these “theories” of VIS directly. Instead, they test:

their own mathematical approximation of the vague theoretical concept, which is often translated differently by each researcher (for an example see the “decision making” literature)
theories from other fields (such as vision science or statistics), or
their own bespoke theory invented for the particular paper.

This leaves the empirical and theoretical work of VIS completely disconnected from one another. Ultimately, VIS is not left with many papers that offer a (correct) theoretical foundation that can be empirically tested.


4. The theories are not recognisable
The disconnect between the empirical and theoretical work at VIS often makes it feel like people are just taking turns saying stuff. However, VIS is not only disconnected from it’s own theories, it is also disconnected from the theories of other fields. I am not an expert in everything, so I can’t speak to every field, however, I am an expert in statistics.
This is all to say, some of the terminology and ideas used by the uncertainty visualisation community are somewhat bizarre. Many of the authors in uncetainty visualisation don’t really seem to know what uncertainty is (which makes their decision to research uncertainty visualisation a little odd if I’m going to be honest). Uncertainty is the by-product of inference, this is just a fact of statistics philosophy and a lot of science philosophy more broadly. Since uncertainty is the by-product of inference it is always connected to some inferential statistic. This means you need to be drawing inference on something for there to be any uncertainty. Additionally, the uncertainty is limited to that one statistic. However, a lot of uncertainty visualisations papers treat uncertainty as a vibe or something that erupted from a nebulous void (e.g. 1, 2). Alternatively they think that uncertainty distributions on different estimates are freely exchangeable (e.g. 1, 2). Or they link the quantification of uncertainty to it’s visualisation approach (e.g. 1 and 2), even though uncertainty really shouldn’t be quantified inside the visualisation.



If I hear this joke one more time I’m going to stab someone.


There are also a lot of VIS papers that are clearly knocking on the door of some very foundational statistics theories, and they would benefit from the specificity that comes with adopting the norms of statistics. For example, there are a few papers that give a taxonomy, or design a perceptual test, for what is fundamentally the statistical issue of bias and variance (e.g. e.g.1, 2, and 3). There is also this recent bluesky thread which boils down to a discussion about the impact of the conflicting assumptions made by a plot designer and it’s viewer, an issue which has a parallel in statistics as multi-phase inference.

title: If VIS wants rigor, it can’t incentivise crackpot science.
section: My suggestions to be less (or more, no judgement here) crackpotty
text:
My suggestions to be less (or more, no judgement here) crackpotty
So, to summarise these issues, VIS has a little bit of crackpottery going on. And look guys, I get it. I have done my fair share of crackpot research.
Ultimately, I think the VIS communities greatest strength is also its biggest weakness, and that is its openness to new ideas that are not (and may never be) fully formed or testable. This openness is what is causing the lack of rigor that has you people crashing out about the field being directionless (see e.g.1 and e.g.2). VIS can’t be desperate for rigor, and then be hostile to rigor itself. So I think its worthwhile to maybe evaluate the openness of the community, and ask yourself if it is always a good thing. When I think about what it is we are trying to do in science, I often think of this quote by Henri Poincaré:

“Science is built up of facts, as a house is built of stones; but an accumulation of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house.”

I often find that, in VIS research, a paper will offer their own bespoke validation of their own bespoke theory. They will toss away an existing house because their brick does not fit in. At the end of the day, you are left looking at a pile of stones, and nobody seems to be building a house. I think (or god, hope) that VIS can be more than this, so I implore the researchers to start thinking about the kind of research that helps to build a house.
In statistics, it is my job to write my theories/arguments that start from the existing literature. If I disagree, I need to (convincingly) explain why, otherwise, I need to build on top of the existing theories. This puts a larger burden on the author, as they must cut and shape their ideas so their brick fits into the existing structure of the house. This comment makes me wonder if the celebration of individualism in VIS is also inhibiting cohesive research. Good science is a collaborative effort, and collaboration in science, just as in life, means limiting our individual freedoms. The same is true for software design (a point I think is made quite well by this comment).
You might read my post, which asks you to cut your stones so they fit in the house, and see it as an affront to the boundary pushing freedom of academic work. But I ask you not to read this from the perspective of an author but from the perspective of a reader. The reader who you have given a pile of stones, many of which do not fit together, many of which cannot fit together even they are presented as though they fit together, and you have told this reader to build a house.
There is a trade off in how accessible your field is to a reader or viewer, to stone maker and house constructor. Do you overburden the reader and force them to spend years navigating conflicting literature (with conversations that are so independent the literature doesn’t acknowledge this conflict)? Are the readers each burdened to build their own house (exacerbating the problem where the field has no common theory)? Or, do you start putting some of the burden on the authors, and ask them to shape their work into something that talks to the existing literature?
Ultimately, from my perspective, the VIS literature (specifically the sub-areas I am adjacent to) either need to:

Stop being so loosy-goosy with what you consider to be research, and start asking for properly defined, and testable theories, or
Fully lean into the openness of everything and anything being research and accept the fact that the literature will not be cohesive, and there will not be a house.

If you want to stop being so loosy goosy, then you need to start formalising your ideas. I don’t care how you do it, use statistics, psychology, information theory, anything would work, but for the love of god, make it something I can use when I need to build an extension on the house. Personally, I would prefer you formalise it in statistics, given the information theory issue I raised above (you can’t perceive information or data that isnt there). Plus, I have seen a few papers that identify a “human” bias, which is actually a statistical bias, so setting a foundation in statistics (at least for data visualisations) would (hopefully) stop that from happening.
A formal theory will not ruin your field. Like, “fields that have a mathematically defined theory that they test” is basically all of science, including fields like physics, economics, and meteorology. I’m not even saying you need formulas, I’m saying be specific enough that it can be tested or discredited. Its not even the bad stuff, really clever experiments are some of the best thing science had to offer. I’m not even saying you can’t do both the theory and the experiment. The theory just needs to be sent to a venue that has the expertise to assess it. If this blog post is evidence of anything, it is evidence that the VIS community clearly cannot be trusted to do their own statistics (no offence).
Or don’t, and just keep doing what you guys are doing. I don’t really care. We all do a little crackpot science.

title: If VIS wants rigor, it can’t incentivise crackpot science.
text:
P.S. the rebuttal & comments
This post generated quite a bit of online discussion, which quickly became difficult to navigate as the replies stacked up. As a firm believer in the merits of academic debate, I think it is important that I platform the rebuttals to this post (of which there were many). Here I link the responses to this post, so you, the reader, may engage with the wider discourse and come to your own conclusions about the merit of the criticism that I levy against the VIS literature. Keep in mind, I update this post to clarify points as the confusions come to my attention. If you are reading this blog post later, and think that it makes a strong point, you, in large part, these rebuttals to thank for that.
I will also add examples to the VIS papers I love, and statistics mistakes to share the love (and hate) wider to avoid individual people feeling attacked or unfairly elevated above their peers.
First, comments from three people I would broadly consider to be statisticians (we are not a monolith, so it is only fair to illustrate that they all don’t agree with me):

Keigan Rice
Cynthia Huang (+ comments from Jonatan Hildén)
Joyce Robbins (who just have positive vibes)

Then a lot of good points from VIS researchers that are worth reading (this list is in no particular oder):
